findings.claim: Adding `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` unconditionally to the generated half of the user's own `partial` resolver class breaks existing code. Inputs: `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver]` or `[CompositeResolver(...)]` on a `partial class` that the user already marked `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`, which is the obvious thing to do for a resolver class. `ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` is `AllowMultiple = false`, so on net5+/netcoreapp targets the merged declaration carries the attribute twice and fails with CS0579. Code that compiled on base no longer compiles. The generator does not check whether the user's declaration already has the attribute.

receipt_plan.detail: Run ExcludeFromCodeCoverageEdgeCaseTests.UserResolverAlreadyExcludedFromCoverage_StillCompiles. Its source is `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver][System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] partial class MyResolver {}` with SkipGeneratedSourcesCheck and no expected diagnostics. Base passes; head fails with CS0579 in the generated MyResolver file. The same applies to CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:7.

findings.claim: The guard `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` drops the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework, which are the most common library targets. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+, so the condition is too broad. On those targets no generated formatter or resolver is excluded from coverage, so 'all generated code is decorated' does not hold. The requirement only allows conditional emission where the attribute does not exist.
